# Introduction
We follow [ISLR (2013)](#r1) pages 46 and 47 for contouring using `ggplot` and `tidyverse` concepts.

# Packages
As usual, we have some standard packages. 
```{r}
library(ISLR2) # some data files
library(mbadtools)
```

# Data
Construct the data with `seq`.
```{r}
x=seq(-pi, pi, length=50)
y=x
```

# Data for Contouring
```{r}
f = outer(x, y, function (x,y)cos(y)/(1+x^2))
```

# Old Contouring
```{r}
contour (x, y, f)
contour (x, y, f, nlevels = 45, add=TRUE)
fa=(f-t(f))/2
contour (x, y, fa, nlevels = 15)
```
# Modern contouring

The modern way:
```{r}
# Put data on a grid
grid <- expand.grid(x = x, y = y)

# A z value for each (x,y)
grid$z <- with(grid, cos(y)/(1+x^2))

# Plot contours
ggplot(grid, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_contour(bins=45) +
  geom_contour_filled()
```

Make a ggplot.
```{r}
#labeling contours
library(metR) # for labeling contours instead of legend
# ggplot
ggplot(grid, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_contour(bins=45) +
  metR::geom_text_contour(breaks = c(-1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1))
```

```{r}
# transformed data
f1 = as.matrix(f)
f2 = t(f1)
grid$za = (as.vector(f1 - f2))/2

# Plot contours
ggplot(grid, aes(x, y, z = za)) +
  geom_contour(bins=45) +
  geom_contour_filled()

#labeling contours
library(metR) # for labeling contours instead of legend
ggplot(grid, aes(x, y, z = za)) +
  geom_contour(bins=45) +
  metR::geom_text_contour(breaks = c(-0.5, 0, 0.5))
```

# Old Heatmap
```{r}
image(x,y, fa)

persp(x,y,fa)

persp(x,y,fa, theta=30)

persp(x,y,fa, theta=30,phi=20)

persp(x,y,fa, theta=30,phi=70)

persp(x,y,fa, theta=30,phi=40)

```

# Modern Heatmap

```{r}
ggplot(grid, aes(x, y, z = za)) +
  geom_contour(bins=45) +
  geom_contour_filled()

ggplot(grid, aes(x, y, fill = za)) +
  geom_raster(interpolate = TRUE) +
  geom_contour(aes(z = za), color = "white") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  coord_equal()
```

# Using `plotly` for surfaces
Here is how to imitate `persp`. There's no need for rotation parameters because you can drag the view around.
```{r}
library(plotly)

plot_ly(x = ~x, y = ~y, z = ~as.matrix(fa)) %>% add_surface()
```

# Conclusion
We found out how to draw contour plots, heat maps, and surfaces the modern tidyverse way.

# References
::: {#r1}
1. ISLR (2013), Chapter 2 Statistical Learning, page 46-47.
